“Thou knowest all things,” meaneth, “things present, and things to come.” Seest thou how he had become better and more sober, being no more self-willed, or contradicting? For on this account he was troubled, “lest perchance I think that I love, and love not, as before when I thought and affirmed much, yet I was convicted at last.” But Jesus asketh him the third time, and the third time giveth him the same injunction, to show at what a price He setteth the care of His own sheep, and that this especially is a sign of love towards Him. And having spoken to him concerning the love towards Himself, He foretelleth to him the martyrdom which he should undergo, showing that He said not to Him what he said as distrusting, but as greatly trusting him; wishing besides to point out a proof of love towards Him, and to instruct us in what manner especially we ought to love Him. Wherefore He saith,

He said this to show by what kind of death Peter would glorify God. After saying this, he told him, “Follow me.”

— John 21:19

J. C. Ryle · Expository Thoughts on John

We have here one of John’s peculiar parenthetical comments, and one for which we may be specially thankful. Who can tell what Commentators might have made of our Lord’s prediction to Peter, if John had not been mercifully inspired to tell us that Jesus spoke of his death?

The expression “what death “means “what kind of death,” and is generally considered to indicate that the preceding verse describes death by crucifixion.

The expression “glorify God “is peculiarly interesting, because it teaches that a Christian may bring glory to God by his death, as well as by his life. He does so when he bears it patiently, does not murmur, exhibits sensible peace, enjoys evident hope of a better world, testifies to others of the truth and consolation of the Gospel, and leaves broad evidences of the reality of his religion behind him. He that so ends glorifies God. The deaths of Latimer, Ridley, Hooper, Bradford, Rogers, Rowland Taylor, and many other English martyrs, in the days of Queen Mary, were said to have done more good even than their lives, and to have had immense influence in helping forward the Protestant Reformation.

The disciple whom Jesus loved

Peter turned around and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the same disciple who at the supper had leaned back against Jesus’s chest and said, “Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?” When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, and what about him?”

— John 21:20–21

John Chrysostom · Homilies on John

Ver. 20, 21. “Then Peter turning about, seeth the disciple whom Jesus loved following; who also leaned on His breast at supper; and saith, Lord, and what shall this man do?”

[2.] Wherefore hath he reminded us of that reclining? Not without cause or in a chance way, but to show us what boldness Peter had after the denial. For he who then did not dare to question Jesus, but committed the office to another, was even entrusted with the chief authority over the brethren, and not only doth not commit to another what relates to himself, but himself now puts a question to his Master concerning another. John is silent, but Peter speaks. He showeth also here the love which he bare towards him; for Peter greatly loved John, as is clear from what followed, and their close union is shown through the whole Gospel, and in the Acts. When therefore Christ had foretold great things to him, and committed the world to him, and spake beforehand of his martyrdom, and testified that his love was greater than that of the others, desiring to have John also to share with him, he said, “And what shall this man do?” “Shall he not come the same way with us?” And as at that other time not being able himself to ask, he puts John forward, so now desiring to make him a return, and supposing that he would desire to ask about the matters pertaining to himself, but had not courage, he himself undertook the questioning. What then saith Christ?

Jesus said to him, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? As for you, follow me!”

— John 21:22

John Wesley · Explanatory Notes

If I will that he tarry — Without dying, till I come — To judgment. Certainly he did tarry, till Christ came to destroy Jerusalem. And who can tell, when or how he died? What is that to thee? — Who art to follow me long before.

So the saying spread among the brothers and sisters that this disciple would not die. But Jesus had not told Peter that the disciple would not die; he had said, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?” This is the disciple who is testifying about these things and who has written them, and we know his testimony is true. Jesus did many other things as well. If each one were written down, I suppose that even the world itself could not hold all the books that would be written.

— John 21:23–25

John Calvin · Commentary on John

There are also many other things that Jesus did. Lest any one should view his narrative with suspicion, as if it had been written through partiality, because Jesus loved him, he anticipates this objection, by saying, that he has passed over more than he has written. He does not speak of Christ’s actions of every kind, but of those which relate to his public office; nor ought we to think that the hyperbole is absurd, when we bear with many figures of speech of the same kind in heathen authors. Not only ought we to take into account the number of Christ’s works, but we ought also to consider their importance and magnitude. The majesty of Christ, which by its infinity swallowed up, if I may so speak, not only the senses of men, but heaven and earth, gave a miraculous display of its own splendor in those works. If the Evangelist, casting his eyes on that brightness, exclaims in astonishment, that even the whole world could not contain a full narrative, ought we to wonder at it? Nor is he at all to be blamed, if he employ a frequent and ordinary figure of speech for commending the excellence of the works of Christ. For we know how God accommodates himself to the ordinary’ way of speaking, on account of our ignorance, and sometimes even, if I may be allowed the expression, stammers.
fields.summary: By the Sea of Tiberias the risen Jesus gives the disciples a huge catch of fish and shares breakfast with them. Three times Jesus asks Peter for his love and tells him to feed the sheep, and the disciple Jesus loved is named as the one who wrote these things. With John Chrysostom, Augustine, John Calvin and 5 more.

fields.title: The Voices and Their Books
fields.body_html:
Eleven people speak in this book, across sixteen centuries. Here is a little about each of them, in the order they lived, and then the edition every excerpt was copied from.

The early Church

Origen (c. 185–c. 253) taught in Alexandria and later in Caesarea, and was the first Christian to study the Bible as a scholar with everything he had. His commentary on John is one of the earliest Christian commentaries on any book of Scripture. Only part of it survives, and only its opening reaches this book, but it is where the chain begins.

John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) was a preacher at Antioch and later archbishop of Constantinople. His name means “golden-mouthed”. His eighty-eight homilies on John were preached to an ordinary congregation, and he never forgets them: he explains the text, then turns to how they are living.

Augustine (354–430), bishop of Hippo in North Africa, preached his way through John in 124 sermons, the Tractates. They are the most personal commentary here: he argues, wonders aloud, and keeps coming back to love.

Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444), bishop of Alexandria, wrote a long commentary on John with a theologian’s eye, always asking what each verse shows about who Christ is.

The Reformation

John Calvin (1509–1564), the reformer of Geneva, published his commentary on John in 1553. He aimed at what he called “lucid brevity”: plain sense first, then its use for faith.

Cornelius a Lapide (1567–1637) was a Flemish Jesuit who taught at Louvain and Rome and wrote commentaries on almost the whole Bible. He gathers the Fathers generously, so through him many older voices reach the chain.

The 1700s

Matthew Henry (1662–1714) was a Presbyterian minister at Chester in England. His commentary on the whole Bible, written to be read at home, has been loved for three centuries for its warmth and its gift for pointing a verse at the heart.

Johann Albrecht Bengel (1687–1752) was a Lutheran scholar in Württemberg. His Gnomon, “pointer”, of 1742 is famously brief: a few words that open a whole verse.

John Wesley (1703–1791), the founder of Methodism, wrote his Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament for ordinary readers and leaned openly on Bengel. His notes are the shortest in this book.

The 1800s

J. C. Ryle (1816–1900), later the first Bishop of Liverpool, wrote his Expository Thoughts on the Gospels for family reading. He draws out a few plain lessons from every passage, and presses them home.

B. F. Westcott (1825–1901), Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge and later Bishop of Durham, wrote one of the most careful commentaries on John in English, first published in 1880. His notes weigh single words.

The editions

Origen, Commentary on the Gospel of John. English translation in Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 9, ed. Allan Menzies (1896-97); the volume names no separate translator for the Commentary on John. 3 excerpts in this book.

John Chrysostom, Homilies on the Gospel of St. John. The Oxford translation (Library of the Fathers), revised and edited by Philip Schaff, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 14 (1889). 53 excerpts in this book.

Augustine of Hippo, Lectures or Tractates on the Gospel According to St. John. Translated by John Gibb and James Innes, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 7 (1888). 56 excerpts in this book.

Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on the Gospel according to S. John. P. E. Pusey (1874) for Books 1-6 to John 8; Thomas Randell (1885) from John 9. 41 excerpts in this book.

John Calvin, Commentary on the Gospel According to John. Translated by William Pringle for the Calvin Translation Society (1847). 78 excerpts in this book.

Cornelius a Lapide, The Great Commentary: S. John's Gospel. English translation by Thomas W. Mossman and others (first published 1876-1887; these are the 1908 Edinburgh printings). Mossman translated John 1-6, James Bliss chapters 7-10, S. J. Eales chapter 11, a Mr. Macpherson chapter 13, and Mossman and Bliss the rest. 19 excerpts in this book.

Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, Volume V (Matthew to John). Matthew Henry, Exposition of the Old and New Testaments (1706-1721), CCEL edition. 57 excerpts in this book.

Johann Albrecht Bengel, Gnomon of the New Testament, Vol. II (Gospels according to St Luke and St John). Translated and edited by Andrew R. Fausset, T&T Clark, Vol. II (1858). 36 excerpts in this book.

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament: St. John. John Wesley, Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (London, 1755), CCEL edition (“Wesley's Notes on the Bible”; CCEL does not name the printing it follows). 38 excerpts in this book.

J. C. Ryle, Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: St. John, Vol. I. Expository Thoughts on the Gospels, for Family and Private Use, with the Text Complete. St. John, Vols. I-III. New York: Robert Carter & Brothers, 1878-79 (American printing of the work first published in London, 1865); archive.org scan “expositorythough05ryle”, djvu OCR text. 75 excerpts in this book.

B. F. Westcott, The Gospel According to St. John: The Authorised Version with Introduction and Notes. London: John Murray, 1892 (“Ninth thousand”), the separate edition reprinted from The Speaker's Commentary (1880); archive.org scan “gospelaccordingt00westuoft” (University of Toronto), djvu OCR text. 37 excerpts in this book.

Every excerpt was gathered by Logia (logia.faith), which copies each one word for word from the public-domain edition above and offers the collection under CC0. The Gospel text is the Open Word Bible (openwordbible.org), English, Balanced level, also CC0.
